blocks.text: Communication skills • Medical ethics • Informed consent • Clinical decision-making
You are an obstetric doctor caring for a pregnant woman who requires an intervention. The examiner asks you to obtain informed consent for one of the following:

items.text: Caesarean section.
Induction of labour.
Blood transfusion.
Operative vaginal delivery using forceps or vacuum.
Manual removal of the placenta.
Evacuation of retained products of conception.
Sterilisation or another contraceptive procedure.
An obstetric procedure where the woman is anxious or reluctant.

blocks.text: Your task is to explain the indication, procedure, benefits, risks, alternatives and consequences of declining treatment, then establish that the woman has made a voluntary, informed decision.
The central principle: Consent is a communication process, not merely a signature on a form.
Informed consent is a voluntary decision made by a patient with the capacity to decide, after receiving and understanding relevant information about a proposed intervention.

items.text: Why the intervention is recommended.
What the procedure involves.
Its expected benefits.
Material risks and possible complications.
Reasonable alternatives, including no intervention where appropriate.
The likely consequences of accepting or declining the intervention.
The opportunity to ask questions and change her mind.

blocks.text: Consent must be obtained before the intervention whenever possible and in accordance with applicable law and institutional policy.

subsections.subsection_title: 3. The essential elements of valid consent

blocks.text: Remember these six elements.
1. Information
Explain the procedure, benefits, material risks, alternatives and consequences of refusal.
2. Capacity
The woman can understand, retain, use or weigh relevant information and communicate a decision.
3. Understanding
Use understandable language and check comprehension rather than simply asking whether she understands.
4. Voluntariness
The decision must be free from coercion, intimidation or inappropriate pressure.
5. Alternatives
Discuss reasonable alternatives, including their benefits and risks.
6. Documentation
Record the discussion, questions, decision, relevant risks and any conditions or limitations.

subsections.subsection_title: 4. Step-by-step approach to an obstetric consent station

blocks.text: “Good morning, Madam. My name is Dr ____. I am one of the doctors looking after you today. I would like to discuss a procedure that we have recommended for you, explain why we think it may help, and talk through the benefits, risks and alternatives. Is that alright?”
Confirm identity and privacy.
Ask what the woman understands about her condition.

items.text: “What have you been told about your condition?”
“What is your understanding of why we have recommended this procedure?”
“What concerns you most about it?”

blocks.text: Correct misconceptions without dismissing her fears.
Describe the problem in plain language.
For example, for an emergency caesarean section:

“Your baby's heart rate is showing concerning changes, and we are worried that your baby may not be coping well with labour. We recommend delivering the baby by caesarean section because we believe this may be the safest way to deliver promptly.”
The explanation must reflect the actual clinical circumstances. Do not exaggerate urgency or promise a particular outcome.

blocks.title: Describe what will happen, where relevant:

items.text: Preparation and monitoring.
Anaesthesia.
Main steps of the procedure.
Expected duration or recovery, if known and relevant.
Post-procedure monitoring and aftercare.

blocks.text: Use diagrams or written materials if they would help.

content_groups.group_title: Step 5: Explain benefits and material risks

blocks.text: Discuss common complications and serious risks that are relevant to the woman and the decision. Explain uncertainty honestly.

Do not overwhelm the patient with an indiscriminate list of every theoretical complication. Focus on risks that a reasonable person in her circumstances would want to know, including risks specific to her clinical history.

items.text: Continued observation.
A different method of delivery.
Another treatment option.
Referral for specialist assessment, where feasible.
No intervention, with an explanation of the likely consequences.

blocks.text: Do not present an alternative as safe or available if it is not clinically reasonable in the actual situation.
Use teach-back:
“Just so I know I have explained everything clearly, could you tell me in your own words what the procedure is intended to do and what the main risks are?”
This checks the clarity of your explanation, not the intelligence of the patient.

content_groups.group_title: Step 8: Invite questions and allow a decision

blocks.text: Ask:
“What questions do you have?”
“Is there anything you would like me to explain again?”
“Do you feel you have enough information to decide?”
Give the woman time when the clinical circumstances permit. Avoid coercion or pressure from family members or staff.

content_groups.group_title: Step 9: Confirm the decision and document

blocks.text: If she agrees, confirm that consent is voluntary and document the discussion according to local policy.
If she declines, explore her concerns, explain relevant risks and alternatives, and respect her informed decision when she has capacity. Continue to provide appropriate care.
Important: Consent can be withdrawn at any time before or during a procedure, subject to the practical realities of stopping safely.
This is a common O&G OSCE station.

blocks.title: Depending on the circumstances, caesarean section may be recommended for:

items.text: Persistent fetal compromise.
Labour that is not progressing despite appropriate management.
Placenta praevia obstructing vaginal birth.
Certain malpresentations, such as transverse lie.
Some cases of previous uterine surgery.
Selected cases of multiple pregnancy.
Other maternal or fetal conditions where vaginal birth is unsafe or less appropriate.

blocks.text: Explain the actual indication rather than reciting a generic list.
Example:

“A caesarean section is an operation in which we deliver your baby through an incision in your abdomen and uterus. It is usually performed under spinal or epidural anaesthesia, although general anaesthesia may sometimes be required. We will monitor you during the operation and provide pain relief afterwards.”

items.text: May permit prompt delivery when vaginal delivery is unsafe or too slow.
Can reduce certain risks associated with the underlying obstetric complication.
May be the safest route of delivery in specific maternal or fetal conditions.

blocks.text: Avoid saying that caesarean section guarantees a healthy baby or eliminates all risks.

items.text: Bleeding and possible blood transfusion.
Infection of the wound or uterus.
Blood clots, including deep-vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism.
Injury to nearby organs, such as the bladder or bowel.
Anaesthetic complications.
Rarely, hysterectomy or life-threatening complications.
Postoperative pain and a longer recovery than uncomplicated vaginal birth.
Increased risks in some future pregnancies, including placenta praevia or placenta accreta spectrum and uterine scar complications.
Accidental skin injury during delivery, which is uncommon.
Respiratory difficulties, particularly when delivered before labour or before the appropriate gestational age.
Potential effects of the underlying condition that necessitated the operation.

blocks.text: Explain that the baby's individual risk depends on gestational age and the clinical circumstances.

items.text: Continued labour with close monitoring.
Assisted vaginal delivery, if appropriate.
Induction or augmentation of labour, where safe.
Another intervention suited to the specific complication.

blocks.text: For a true emergency, explain clearly why there may be insufficient time for an alternative.

“Madam, because of the changes we are seeing in your baby's condition, we recommend a caesarean section. This means delivering your baby through an operation involving cuts in your abdomen and uterus.
The main benefit is that it may allow us to deliver your baby more quickly and safely in the present circumstances.

The risks include bleeding, infection, blood clots, injury to nearby organs and complications from anaesthesia. Serious complications are uncommon but can occur. The operation also has implications for recovery and some future pregnancies.
Depending on your baby's condition and how labour is progressing, there may be alternatives, but I will explain whether any of them are safe in your particular situation.
What questions or concerns do you have? Would you like me to explain any part again?”
Induction of labour is the process of initiating labour artificially before it begins spontaneously, when delivery is considered appropriate.

items.text: Pregnancy continuing beyond the recommended gestational period.
Prelabour rupture of membranes in appropriate circumstances.
Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy.
Selected maternal medical conditions.
Concerns about fetal wellbeing where delivery is indicated.

blocks.title: Depending on the clinical situation and local protocol:

items.text: Cervical ripening with medication, such as a prostaglandin.
Mechanical cervical ripening with a balloon catheter.
Amniotomy, when appropriate.
Oxytocin infusion.

blocks.text: Explain which method or sequence is proposed for the individual patient.

items.text: Initiates delivery when continuing the pregnancy may pose greater risks.
May reduce risks associated with prolonged pregnancy or certain maternal and fetal conditions.
May allow vaginal birth and avoid caesarean section, although induction can sometimes lead to operative delivery.
Painful or prolonged induction.
Failure to establish labour, sometimes requiring caesarean section.
Uterine hyperstimulation, particularly with some medications, which may affect the baby's heart rate.
Need for continuous or additional fetal monitoring.
Uterine rupture, a rare but important risk in selected circumstances, particularly with a previous uterine scar.
Infection or other complications depending on the clinical circumstances.
Expectant management with an appropriate monitoring plan, if safe.
Another method of induction.
Caesarean delivery, where indicated.

blocks.text: Explain the risks of continuing the pregnancy as well as the risks of induction.

“We recommend induction because we believe it is safer for you and your baby to deliver now than to continue the pregnancy. We would use a method to help your cervix prepare for labour and may use other methods to start contractions.

The process may take several hours or longer. It can be uncomfortable, may not succeed and may sometimes lead to caesarean delivery. Some medications can cause contractions that are too frequent, which is why monitoring is important.
We will discuss the most suitable method for you, the alternatives and what may happen if you choose to wait.”
This may arise in postpartum haemorrhage, severe anaemia or another serious obstetric complication.

blocks.title: Explain why transfusion is being considered:

items.text: Significant blood loss.
Haemodynamic instability.
Severe symptomatic anaemia.
Other clinically significant deficiencies requiring blood components.

blocks.text: The indication depends on the woman's condition, haemoglobin level, ongoing bleeding and other clinical factors.

items.text: Restores circulating red blood cells and improves oxygen delivery.
Supports resuscitation in major bleeding.
May prevent organ injury or death when clinically necessary.

blocks.text: Explain that transfusion is generally safe when properly indicated and administered, but risks include:

items.text: Fever or allergic reactions.
Haemolytic transfusion reactions.
Transfusion-associated circulatory overload.
Transfusion-related acute lung injury.
A very small residual risk of transmitting infections despite donor screening.
Other complications depending on the clinical circumstances.

blocks.title: Where clinically reasonable, alternatives may include:

items.text: Treating the underlying cause of blood loss.
Iron therapy for suitable cases of iron-deficiency anaemia.
Measures to minimise further bleeding.
Other blood conservation approaches.

blocks.text: In major haemorrhage or life-threatening anaemia, these alternatives may not provide a sufficiently rapid or effective replacement for transfusion.
“Your blood count and clinical condition indicate that you may benefit from a blood transfusion. The purpose is to replace blood components and improve the delivery of oxygen to your organs.

Most transfusions are given without serious complications, but reactions can occur. These include fever, allergy and, rarely, serious reactions affecting the lungs or circulation. The risk of transmitting infection is very low because donated blood is screened.
We will explain any reasonable alternatives in your situation. What concerns do you have about receiving blood?”

If the woman declines transfusion, explore her concerns respectfully, explain the risks of refusal, document her decision and develop an appropriate alternative plan where possible. Do not assume that a relative can override a competent adult's refusal.
Forceps or vacuum extraction may be considered when assisted vaginal birth is clinically appropriate.

items.text: Delay in the second stage of labour.
Concern about fetal condition when expedited vaginal birth is appropriate.
Maternal conditions where shortening the pushing phase may be beneficial.
May achieve vaginal birth more quickly.
May avoid or reduce the need for a second-stage caesarean section in appropriate circumstances.
Perineal tears, including severe tears.
Vaginal or cervical trauma.
Postpartum bleeding.
Pain and pelvic floor injury.

blocks.title: Depending on the instrument and circumstances:

items.text: Bruising or superficial injuries.
Cephalohaematoma or other scalp injury, particularly with vacuum extraction.
Facial injury or nerve injury, particularly with forceps.
Rarely, serious neonatal injury.
Continue pushing, if safe.
Caesarean section.
Another appropriate method of assisted delivery, where suitable.

blocks.text: The choice depends on the fetal position, station, urgency, operator skill and clinical circumstances.

“We are considering assisting your baby's birth with an instrument because we believe this may help deliver the baby more safely or quickly. The instrument would be applied to your baby's head to help guide delivery.

The benefits are that we may achieve vaginal birth more quickly. The risks include tears and bleeding for you, and bruising or other injury to the baby. If the attempt is unsuccessful, we may need to proceed to caesarean section.
I will explain why we recommend this option and whether continuing to push or caesarean section would be reasonable alternatives in your situation.”

subsections.subsection_title: 9. Consent for manual removal of the placenta

blocks.text: The placenta has not delivered and manual removal is considered necessary, for example, because of retained placenta or associated bleeding.
The clinician removes the placenta manually from the uterus, usually with appropriate anaesthesia or analgesia and aseptic precautions.

items.text: Removes retained placental tissue.
May control bleeding and reduce the risk of ongoing haemorrhage or infection.
Pain and anaesthetic complications.
Bleeding.
Infection.
Uterine injury or perforation, rarely.
Failure to remove the placenta completely.
Further intervention, including surgery, in complicated cases.

blocks.text: Important: Suspected placenta accreta spectrum may make attempted manual removal hazardous and requires appropriate specialist planning.
“Your placenta has not come out, and we are concerned about the risk of bleeding and other complications if it remains inside the uterus. We recommend removing it manually.

This usually requires appropriate anaesthesia or pain relief. The risks include bleeding, infection and, rarely, injury to the uterus. If the placenta is abnormally attached, the management may need to be different.
I will explain the plan and answer your questions before proceeding, unless an emergency changes what is possible.”
This is a high-yield ethics question.

content_groups.group_title: A. How do you assess decision-making capacity?

blocks.title: For the specific decision, assess whether the woman can:

items.text: Understand the relevant information.
Retain it long enough to make the decision.
Use or weigh the information as part of the decision.
Communicate her choice.

blocks.text: Capacity is decision-specific and may fluctuate. A diagnosis, disability, disagreement with the doctor or an apparently unwise decision does not by itself establish incapacity.

content_groups.group_title: B. What if the woman refuses a recommended intervention?

items.text: Explore her reasons and concerns.
Ensure she has received clear, balanced information.
Correct misunderstandings.
Discuss alternatives and the consequences of refusal.
Offer a second opinion or senior review where feasible.
Respect an informed decision by a woman with capacity.
Document the discussion and continue appropriate care.

blocks.text: Pregnancy does not remove a competent adult's right to refuse treatment.

content_groups.group_title: C. What if she lacks capacity and the situation is an emergency?

blocks.text: Follow applicable law and professional guidance. Where immediate treatment is necessary to prevent serious harm and the patient cannot make the decision, clinicians may need to act in her best interests or under the applicable emergency legal framework.
Provide the least restrictive appropriate intervention, document the basis for action and involve senior clinicians as soon as practicable.
Do not assume that a partner or relative automatically has authority to consent for an adult who has capacity.

content_groups.group_title: D. What if she is in severe pain or distress?

blocks.text: Treat pain and distress, use clear and brief explanations, and reassess capacity if needed. Urgency may affect how much time is available, but it does not remove the obligation to communicate and obtain consent whenever possible.
Shared decision-making combines the clinician's medical expertise with the woman's values, preferences and circumstances.

items.text: Explain the clinical problem.
Present reasonable options.
Compare benefits and risks.
Ask what matters most to the woman.
Check her understanding.
Agree on a plan where possible.
Document the decision and review it if circumstances change.

blocks.text: A woman with a previous caesarean section asks whether she can attempt vaginal birth.

Rather than immediately deciding for her, explain the suitability criteria, probability of successful vaginal birth, relevant risks, possibility of emergency caesarean section and the availability of appropriate monitoring and emergency services.
The final recommendation should be individualised to her obstetric history and clinical circumstances.

items.text: Patient identity and the proposed intervention.
Indication and relevant clinical findings.
Benefits and material risks discussed.
Reasonable alternatives and consequences of refusal.
Questions asked and information provided.
Evidence of understanding and voluntariness.
Decision made, including any refusal or limitations.
Date, time and names of relevant clinicians.
The consent form, where required by local policy.

blocks.text: A signed form alone does not prove that informed consent occurred.
For an urgent procedure, document the clinical urgency, the discussion undertaken, the patient's decision and any limitations imposed by the emergency.

subsections.subsection_title: 13. Common examiner questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is the difference between consent and assent?

Consent is a legally and ethically valid authorisation by a person with the relevant decision-making authority and capacity. Assent is an affirmative agreement from someone who may not have full legal authority to provide consent, often used in paediatric care alongside the required consent process.
Q2. Can a woman withdraw consent after signing the form?
Yes. She can withdraw consent before or during the procedure. The clinician should stop if it is safe and feasible to do so, explain the situation and reassess the plan.
Q3. Is written consent always required?

Not for every clinical intervention. Requirements depend on the procedure, circumstances, applicable law and institutional policy. Major procedures generally require formal documentation, but verbal consent may be appropriate for some interventions.
Q4. Does a signature prove informed consent?
No. The clinician must ensure the patient received and understood relevant information and made a voluntary decision.
Q5. What if a patient makes a decision the clinician considers unwise?
If the patient has capacity and is adequately informed, the decision should generally be respected. The clinician should explore concerns, clarify risks and continue to offer appropriate care.
Q6. Can a husband consent to a caesarean section on behalf of his competent wife?
Not as a substitute for her consent. A competent adult woman makes decisions about her own treatment. Her partner may participate if she wishes.
Q7. What is material risk?

A risk is material when a reasonable person in the patient's position would likely consider it significant, or when the clinician knows or should know that the particular patient would consider it significant.
Q8. What if there is no time to obtain consent in a life-threatening emergency?

If the patient lacks capacity and immediate treatment is necessary, follow the applicable emergency legal and professional framework. If she has capacity, her informed decision remains central even in an emergency.
Q9. Why should alternatives be discussed?
Alternatives allow the patient to compare reasonable options and make an informed decision consistent with her preferences and clinical circumstances.
Q10. What is the difference between informed consent and shared decision-making?

Informed consent is the process of authorising a specific intervention after adequate information. Shared decision-making is the broader collaborative process of selecting among reasonable options. They overlap but are not identical.

items.text: Asking the woman to sign before explaining the procedure.
Using technical terms without explanation.
Listing risks without explaining the indication or benefits.
Omitting alternatives and the consequences of declining treatment.
Pressuring the woman by using fear or guilt.
Assuming the partner has decision-making authority.
Treating disagreement as evidence of incapacity.
Failing to check understanding.
Promising that complications will not occur.
Forgetting that consent may be withdrawn.
Relying on a signed form without documenting the discussion.

blocks.text: Clinical indication
Explain why the intervention is being recommended.
Options
Describe reasonable alternatives and the consequences of declining treatment.
Nature of the procedure
Explain what will happen.
Significant risks and benefits
Discuss the benefits, material risks and uncertainties.
Evaluate understanding
Use teach-back and answer questions.
No coercion
Confirm voluntariness and respect the patient's autonomy.
Trace the discussion
Document the information given and the patient's decision.

Final OSCE tip: A strong consent station ends with the patient demonstrating understanding, having the opportunity to ask questions, and making a voluntary decision. The clinician's role is to inform, recommend and support—not to coerce.
